title: Binary Search Fundamentals
summary: Binary search halves the search space every step by maintaining one strict invariant — get that invariant precise and every boundary-search variant (lower_bound, upper_bound, rotated arrays) becomes a small, safe extension.

slides.markdown:
Binary search halves the remaining search space every step by comparing the middle element against a target — O(log n) instead of a linear O(n) scan. Everyone can state that in one sentence; almost everyone still gets the implementation wrong under pressure, because the algorithm's correctness rests entirely on one precise, easy-to-violate **invariant**.

Get that invariant right and every variant — first/last occurrence among duplicates, rotated arrays, "binary search on the answer" — is a small, mechanical extension of the same loop. Get it wrong and you get an off-by-one, an infinite loop, or a silently missed match.

slides.sectionTitle: The invariant: what stays true every iteration
slides.markdown:
The invariant binary search maintains: **if the target exists in the array, it is somewhere within the current `[lo, hi]` window.** Every iteration either finds the target directly, or narrows `[lo, hi]` while provably keeping the target inside it (if it exists at all).

Everything else in the implementation — which half to discard, whether to include or exclude the midpoint, when the loop terminates — falls directly out of preserving this one statement. Losing sight of it (thinking in terms of "move lo" and "move hi" mechanically, without checking each move still respects the invariant) is where off-by-one bugs come from.

slides.sectionTitle: The search window shrinking to nothing
slides.markdown:
![A 16-element array with the lo-hi bracket shrinking roughly in half across four iterations as one side is discarded each time](assets/binary-search-window-shrink.svg)

The visual should make halving concrete: after k iterations, the window size is roughly n / 2^k, so it takes only about log₂(n) iterations to shrink any window down to a single element — for a million-element array, that's about 20 iterations, not a million.

slides.sectionTitle: lower_bound and upper_bound: searching for a boundary
slides.markdown:
Plain binary search answers "does the target exist, and if so where." A different, equally common question: "where's the **boundary**" — the first position where a condition (like `arr[i] >= target`) becomes true. `lower_bound` finds the first index where `arr[i] >= target`; `upper_bound` finds the first index where `arr[i] > target`. Neither requires the target to actually be present in the array.

The invariant shifts slightly: instead of "the target might be in `[lo, hi]`," it becomes "the answer (the boundary index) is somewhere in `[lo, hi]`" — and every iteration narrows toward that boundary rather than toward a specific value's location.

`(lo + hi) / 2` has a classic bug in fixed-width integer languages: if `lo` and `hi` are both large (near the maximum representable integer), their sum can **overflow** before the division happens, wrapping around to a negative or garbage value and corrupting `mid` entirely.

`lo + (hi - lo) / 2` avoids this because `hi - lo` is always the (small) window size, never anywhere near the overflow threshold even when `lo` and `hi` themselves are huge — the subtraction happens first, keeping every intermediate value bounded by the actual search range rather than by the absolute magnitude of the indices. This specific bug famously existed in a real production binary search implementation for years before being caught, which is part of why it's a standard interview detail to get right.

| | Inclusive `[lo, hi]` | Half-open `[lo, hi)` |
|---|---|---|
| Loop condition | `while lo <= hi` | `while lo < hi` |
| Initial hi | `len(arr) - 1` | `len(arr)` |
| Narrowing on "too small" | `lo = mid + 1` | `lo = mid + 1` |
| Narrowing on "too big / could be answer" | `hi = mid - 1` | `hi = mid` |

Both conventions are correct and both are common in real code — the danger is **mixing them**: using `hi = mid` (half-open style) with `while lo <= hi` (inclusive style) can produce an infinite loop, because `hi = mid` doesn't shrink the window when `lo == mid == hi`. Pick one convention per function and apply it consistently.

The difference between O(n) and O(log n) sounds abstract until you put in real numbers. Searching a million-element sorted array: a linear scan touches up to a million elements; binary search touches at most **20** (log₂ 1,000,000 ≈ 20). At a billion elements, linear scan is a billion touches; binary search is **30**.

This is why binary search shows up everywhere real systems care about latency at scale: database index lookups, searching a sorted log for a timestamp range, `bisect`-style standard library functions — anywhere "sorted and searched repeatedly" applies, the log n factor is the difference between a lookup that's instant and one that visibly lags.

The most common binary search bug: using `<` where the convention calls for `<=`, or vice versa, in either the loop condition or the narrowing steps — usually while copy-adapting a template from a different problem (say, adapting a plain-search template into a `lower_bound` without updating every comparison consistently). The result is either an off-by-one wrong answer, a missed boundary case (the target at index 0 or the last index), or in the worst case an infinite loop.

The reliable defense: don't debug by trial and error on comparison operators — write down the loop invariant explicitly first ("the answer is in `[lo, hi]`" or "`[lo, hi)`"), then derive each comparison from what keeps that invariant true, the same way the earlier slides derived them.

Binary search's correctness assumes the array is sorted by **the same key** you're searching on — running it on data sorted by a different field, or on data that merely looks sorted for the values you happened to test, silently produces wrong results rather than an error. A classic version: an array of objects sorted by `id`, searched via binary search using a comparator on `name` — the algorithm runs, returns *some* index, and that index is meaningless.

The fix is a habit, not a code change: before reaching for binary search, explicitly confirm (out loud, in an interview) what field the data is sorted by and that it matches the field being searched on.
